claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of HEAs is governed by shear-induced dynamic amorphization.
Sliding-induced high-strain-rate shear refines a coarse surface into an amorphous/nanocrystalline layer.
The transformed surface layer has a higher defect density than the initial coarse-grained surface.
Refinement and amorphization alter passive-film formation, kinetics, or integrity.
Introducing stress and grain refinement can reduce the corrosion resistance of a Cantor alloy.
The amorphous/nanocrystalline surface layer has lower shear strength than the coarse-grained surface.
Lower surface shear strength caused by the transformed layer reduces friction and wear.
Relative to a coarse-grained baseline, the overall wear rate and friction coefficient should decrease.
The corrosion component could increase if the refined surface supports a less stable passive film.
The corrosion component could decrease if the refined surface promotes a more uniform passive film.
Net tribo-corrosion degradation is likely to be reduced under an optimal mechanical-electrochemical balance.
An additively manufactured HEA can initially be coarse-grained and single-phase.
The proposed initial alloy has a well-developed passive film under static conditions.
The mechanism should operate only when contact stress and strain rate are sufficient to produce substantial surface transformation.
The mechanism may fail when the environment stabilizes the passive film independently of surface microstructure.
Comparing corrosive sliding with otherwise identical inert-environment sliding isolates the chemical contribution to degradation.
Absence of a significantly refined amorphous/nanocrystalline layer would falsify the proposed mediator.
Absence of differences in passive-film stability, friction, and wear between corrosive and inert sliding would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as retaining an unaltered coarse-grained structure during non-corrosive sliding, but the mechanism states that sliding shear itself causes refinement and amorphization. The proposed inert-sliding control therefore may also develop the mediator and is not necessarily an unaltered structural baseline.

The predicted outcome is stated relative to a coarse-grained baseline, whereas the actual experiment compares corrosive sliding with inert sliding. This changes environmental chemistry rather than independently controlling the transformed surface structure, and a static control cannot provide a matched wear comparison.

The boundary says the hypothesis does not apply when sliding fails to induce sufficient transformation, but the falsification rule treats failure to form the transformed layer as falsification. Without a predefined shear condition known to lie inside the claimed domain, that result would indicate an out-of-scope test rather than decisively refute the mechanism.
